tool:unroot.name: unroot
tool:unroot.title: unroot
tool:unroot.short_help: unroot - enter, run, and transport Linux root filesystems
tool:unroot.description:
`unroot` is a small, daemonless tool for trusted build, packaging, cross-architecture, and rootfs-maintenance work. It combines Linux namespaces, durable ownership metadata, and optional QEMU user-mode emulation without requiring a resident container service.

Root filesystem ownership is explicit:

* A *managed rootfs* created by `unroot unpack` uses a rich subordinate UID and GID map by default. It preserves normal multi-user ownership while ordinary entry remains unprivileged.
* A *native rootfs* uses host ownership directly. Create one with `sudo unroot unpack --native`, or explicitly enter an existing host-owned or mounted rootfs with `sudo unroot enter --native`.
* `unroot enter --single ROOT` enters an unmanaged rootfs with only the invoking UID and GID mapped to namespace ID 0. It requires no subordinate IDs, but cannot represent multiple rootfs identities.

These modes are intentionally not fallbacks for one another. A multi-user rootfs is never silently reduced to one identity, and a request for unprivileged operation never silently becomes a host-root operation.

In practical terms, `unroot` supports several useful workflows:

* *A single-owner rootfs without host root.* `unroot enter --single ROOT` changes `/` while mapping only the invoking host user and group to root. It is useful for rootfs trees whose relevant files all belong to that user; a real multi-user rootfs requires rich ownership instead.
* *A sudo-less chroot.* Configure subordinate IDs once, create a rootfs with `unroot unpack`, and enter it later without `sudo`. UID and GID 0 map to the invoking user; the remaining rootfs identities map to the user's subordinate ranges.
* *A direct chroot replacement.* `--native` operates on ordinary host-owned filesystems, NFS-mounted root filesystems, and disposable VM roots without shifting ownership. It requires host root privileges because it deliberately does not create a user namespace.
* *Cross-architecture development.* Enter ARM64 from x86-64, x86-64 from ARM64, or RISC-V from either. `unroot` inspects the requested executable or shebang interpreter and connects it to the matching static QEMU user-mode emulator.
* *Portable rootfs workflows.* `unpack` restores a complete rootfs under its chosen ownership model; `pack` captures it again while preserving numeric owners and extended filesystem metadata.
* *Single-process rootfs execution.* Run one command with a different `/` and private PID and mount state, with no resident container daemon. This is useful for trusted services, build steps, and maintenance tools.
* *Architecture and distribution testing.* Keep a collection of rootfs archives and exercise software against multiple Linux environments without booting a VM for each one.

topic:synopsis.name: synopsis
topic:synopsis.title: SYNOPSIS
topic:synopsis.description:
```text
unroot unpack [--id-count COUNT] ARCHIVE ROOT
sudo unroot unpack --native ARCHIVE ROOT
unroot enter ROOT [OPTIONS] [-- COMMAND [ARGUMENTS...]]
unroot enter --single ROOT [OPTIONS] [-- COMMAND [ARGUMENTS...]]
sudo unroot enter --native ROOT [OPTIONS] [-- COMMAND [ARGUMENTS...]]
unroot pack ROOT ARCHIVE
unroot inject list ROOT [--json]
unroot inject add ROOT ITEM [ITEM...]
unroot inject remove ROOT ITEM [ITEM...]
unroot inject clear ROOT
unroot inspect host [--json]
unroot inspect archive ARCHIVE [--json]
```

topic:quick-start.name: quick-start
topic:quick-start.title: QUICK START
topic:quick-start.description:
Create a faithful multi-user rootfs from an archive, then enter it:

```console
$ unroot unpack alpine.tar.zst ~/rootfs
$ unroot enter ~/rootfs
```

`unpack` requires subordinate UID and GID allocations. It checks the allocation and mapping helpers before creating *ROOT*, so an incomplete host setup does not leave behind a partially initialized destination.

Run a specific command with an explicit environment:

```console
$ unroot enter ~/rootfs \
    --cwd /build \
    --env MAKEFLAGS=-j8 \
    -- make
```

Enter an existing host-owned or NFS-mounted Raspberry Pi rootfs from an x86-64 workstation:

```console
$ sudo unroot enter --native /mnt/raspi4-root -- /bin/sh
```

The explicit `--native` selects host ownership and authorizes any host-global foreign-execution setup required for this boot. The rootfs is not modified with Unroot metadata merely because it was entered.

Enter an unmanaged, single-owner rootfs without subordinate ID allocations:

```console
$ unroot enter --single ~/rootfs -- /bin/sh
```

Only files owned by the invoking host user and group appear as root-owned in this mode. Use a managed rich root when the rootfs must represent other users or groups.

Capture a managed rootfs after modifying it:

```console
$ unroot pack ~/rootfs alpine-modified.tar.zst
```

The archive is host-independent, while its binaries retain the rootfs's target architecture. On another supported Linux host, `unroot` either runs them natively or selects the matching QEMU emulator.

topic:rootfs-archives.name: rootfs-archives
topic:rootfs-archives.title: ROOTFS ARCHIVES
topic:rootfs-archives.description:
Unroot currently supports raw root filesystem tar archives. Filesystem entries such as `bin/`, `etc/`, `usr/`, and `var/` must appear directly at the archive root; Gentoo and Funtoo stage tarballs are common examples. Unroot does not currently strip a wrapping directory or import OCI/container-image layouts, disk images, installer media, or distribution-specific bundles. Additional formats may be supported in the future.

`unroot unpack` creates *ROOT* when needed and extracts *ARCHIVE* under a durable ownership model. The default rich mode maps rootfs ID 0 to the invoking user and IDs 1 through 65535 to that user's subordinate UID and GID ranges. `--id-count COUNT` selects a larger or smaller subordinate extent when the archive needs different ownership headroom. *COUNT* excludes rootfs ID 0, so `--id-count 100000` represents logical IDs 0 through 100000. This preserves a conventional multi-user Linux filesystem without requiring host root privileges after the one-time host allocation is configured.

`sudo unroot unpack --native` instead writes archive ownership directly to the host filesystem. Native mode is appropriate for ordinary privileged chroots, disposable VMs, and filesystems that must retain their existing host-visible numeric ownership.

Both forms write the selected mode and, for rich roots, the exact kernel UID and GID extents to `ROOT/.unroot/meta.json`. Existing metadata is authoritative when unpacking into an otherwise empty initialized rootfs. With no `--id-count`, its recorded count is reused; an explicitly conflicting mode or count is rejected.

After extraction, `unpack` installs writable copies of the host's `/etc/hosts` and `/etc/resolv.conf`, plus an `/etc/mtab` link to `/proc/self/mounts`, by default. Their portable rootfs originals are preserved for later restoration and packing. See *ROOTFS INJECTIONS* for the complete lifecycle and for `--inject` controls that disable any default.

`unroot pack` requires a managed rootfs and validates its recorded ownership model before capture. Archive operations use the sibling `unroot-util` linked to the host's libarchive. The helper runs inside Unroot's selected namespaces with *ROOT* as its working directory, but is not chrooted, so no shell or archive tool is required inside *ROOT*. Destination suffixes select compression filters such as `.gz`, `.xz`, and `.zst` when supported by the host libarchive.

Only one `pack`, `unpack`, or `inject` operation may manage a rootfs at a time. These actions take an exclusive operating-system lock on the pinned root directory and fail immediately when another rootfs-management operation is active. Process exit automatically releases the lock, with no lock file to become stale. `enter` does not mutate the injection registry and does not require this lock.

`pack` records the numeric ownership visible inside the managed root rather than its shifted host representation. The archive can therefore be unpacked under a different ownership model. To create a conventional host-root-owned copy of a rich rootfs:

```console
$ unroot pack ~/roots/gentoo-rich gentoo.tar.zst
$ sudo unroot unpack --native gentoo.tar.zst ~/roots/gentoo-native
```

The reverse works for a managed native root: run `sudo unroot pack` on that root, then use ordinary `unroot unpack` to create a rich unprivileged copy. Conversion always creates a separate destination tree; it does not recursively rewrite the source rootfs or its metadata.

Both actions preserve numeric ownership, permissions, timestamps, symbolic and hard links, sparse files, POSIX ACLs, and extended attributes including file capabilities. SELinux labels are included when SELinux is active. The host-specific top-level `.unroot` tree is excluded from output archives, and an input archive containing that reserved tree is rejected.

Unroot's ACL contract is limited to POSIX ACLs, matching the supported tar metadata path. It does not interpret NFSv4 ACL semantics. Any filesystem-specific representation carried as an extended attribute remains opaque xattr metadata and follows the extended-attribute preservation path.

Before modifying a rootfs, Unroot opens and pins the input archive and performs a complete metadata inspection. Unsafe paths, the reserved `.unroot` tree, OCI image layouts, malformed archives, and ownership outside the selected ID map are rejected before extraction. When that inspection finds POSIX ACLs or extended attributes, Unroot performs a quick capability check on the exact destination filesystem and rejects an incompatible destination before extraction. This check does not reopen or rescan the archive. Recoverable metadata limitations fail closed by default; use `--force` only when the resulting reduction in archive fidelity is understood and acceptable.

Unpacking is intentionally not an overlay operation: *ROOT* must be new or empty apart from valid `.unroot` metadata. A failed extraction may leave a partially populated rootfs for inspection or removal, but structural, ownership, and required destination-capability checks complete before extraction starts.

topic:inspection.name: inspection
topic:inspection.title: INSPECTION
topic:inspection.description:
`unroot inspect host` reports current kernel, namespace, mapping-helper, host-helper, and archive-engine capabilities without changing a rootfs. Availability, confirmed unavailability, and an inconclusive probe are reported separately. Use `--json` for a structured support report.

`unroot inspect archive ARCHIVE` scans a pinned archive without extracting it. It reports the format and compression filters, member and byte counts, maximum numeric UID and GID, rootfs layout markers, and noteworthy metadata such as ACLs, extended attributes, capabilities, SELinux labels, sparse files, links, devices, FIFOs, and sockets. The same inspection path supplies the mandatory safety and ownership checks used by `unpack`.

```console
$ unroot inspect host
$ unroot inspect archive stage3.tar.xz --json
```

topic:injection-lifecycle.name: injection-lifecycle
topic:injection-lifecycle.title: Defaults and lifecycle
topic:injection-lifecycle.description:
`unroot unpack` installs three named injections after creating a managed rootfs. `hosts` and `resolv.conf` are ordinary writable mode-`0644` copies of the host's corresponding files, owned by root inside the rootfs rather than bind-mounted. `mtab` is a root-owned `/etc/mtab` symlink to `/proc/self/mounts`, giving traditional mount-table readers the namespace's live view. Together these defaults provide working host naming, DNS configuration, and mount reporting without exposing host inode ownership.

Before replacing a destination, Unroot preserves its original regular file, symlink, or absence under `ROOT/.unroot/injections/`. That original is captured once. Re-adding an existing injection refreshes the live copy while retaining the same preserved original. Injections remain in place across any number of `enter` commands; `enter` neither applies nor restores them.

Disable defaults while creating a rootfs with a subtractive `--inject` value. A comma-separated value may disable several names, and `-*` disables all current defaults:

```console
$ unroot unpack --inject=-hosts stage3.tar.xz ~/rootfs
$ unroot unpack --inject=-hosts,-mtab stage3.tar.xz ~/rootfs
$ unroot unpack --inject=-* stage3.tar.xz ~/rootfs
```

`unpack --inject` accepts exclusions only. This keeps rootfs creation predictable; add or alter injections afterward with the `inject` action.

topic:injection-management.name: injection-management
topic:injection-management.title: Inspecting and managing injections
topic:injection-management.description:
The `inject` action operates only on managed root filesystems created by `unroot unpack`; it does not modify unmanaged trees used with `enter --single` or `enter --native`.

List the registered injections in a rootfs, optionally as JSON:

```console
$ unroot inject list ~/rootfs
$ unroot inject list ~/rootfs --json
```

Add or refresh any built-in by name:

```console
$ unroot inject add ~/rootfs hosts resolv.conf mtab
```

Custom items use `SOURCE[:DESTINATION[:UID:GID:MODE]]`. With no destination, the same absolute path is used inside *ROOT*. Ownership defaults to `0:0` and mode to `0644`; overridden IDs are IDs inside the rootfs, and mode is octal:

```console
$ unroot inject add ~/rootfs /etc/localtime
$ unroot inject add ~/rootfs /host/config:/etc/example/config:0:0:0600
```

Custom sources may be regular files or symlinks that resolve to regular files. Directories and special files are rejected. The destination parent must already exist. The destination itself may be a regular file, a symlink, or absent; custom injections install regular files, while the built-in `mtab` injection installs its documented symlink. Host source paths are supplied by the current command and are not stored in the rootfs registry.

Remove registrations by built-in name or absolute destination. Removal restores the preserved regular file or symlink, or removes the live copy when the destination was originally absent. `clear` does this for every registration:

```console
$ unroot inject remove ~/rootfs hosts /etc/example/config
$ unroot inject clear ~/rootfs
```

topic:injection-portability.name: injection-portability
topic:injection-portability.title: Packing and concurrency
topic:injection-portability.description:
`unroot pack` does not alter the live rootfs. While creating the archive, it excludes each live injected file or link and substitutes the preserved original at that path. If the path was originally absent, it remains absent from the archive. Host DNS, host names, the generated mount-table link, and custom injected content therefore do not leak into a portable rootfs archive.

The injection registry and preserved originals are private Unroot metadata and are excluded from archives. `pack`, `unpack`, and every `inject` operation share one rootfs lock. File installation and replacement are atomic, while ordinary concurrent `enter` operations only observe the current durable files and never perform competing injection cleanup.

topic:command-selection.name: command-selection
topic:command-selection.title: Command selection
topic:command-selection.description:
Absolute commands are interpreted inside the selected root filesystem. Commands containing a slash are executed relative to `--cwd`, or `/` in rooted mode when no working directory is specified.

A bare command name is resolved with Unroot's deterministic target `PATH`: `/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin`. Unroot never imports the host `PATH` implicitly.

Scripts are supported. For architecture detection, `unroot` follows the script's shebang and inspects the actual interpreter rather than assuming that the requested file is an ELF executable.

If no command is supplied, `enter` runs `/bin/sh`.

topic:environment.name: environment
topic:environment.title: Environment
topic:environment.description:
The target command does not inherit the host environment by default. Unroot supplies a deterministic target `PATH` and, when it is set on the host, preserves `TERM` automatically so interactive terminal programs keep a usable terminal type. `PATH` can be replaced, and any other value can be added, with repeatable `--env KEY=VALUE` options:

```console
$ unroot enter ~/rootfs --env PATH=/bin:/usr/bin -- make
```

Use `--persist-env` to select existing host variables by name:

```console
$ unroot enter ~/rootfs --persist-env TERM,MAKEFLAGS -- /bin/sh
```

An explicit `--env` value wins when the same name also appears in `--persist-env`. Names requested through `--persist-env` but absent from the host are ignored.

Use `--no-default-env` to suppress the built-in `PATH`. Explicit `--env` and `--persist-env` selections still apply. A bare command cannot be resolved when `PATH` is absent or empty, so use an absolute command in a deliberately pathless environment.

topic:ownership-model.name: ownership-model
topic:ownership-model.title: Rootfs ownership
topic:ownership-model.description:
A managed rootfs has an authoritative ownership record in `.unroot/meta.json`:

* *Rich ownership* uses a user namespace. Rootfs ID 0 maps to the invoking host user, and one contiguous subordinate range represents IDs 1 through 65535 by default. `unroot unpack --id-count COUNT` selects different headroom when the account has sufficiently large subordinate UID and GID allocations.
* *Native ownership* uses host IDs unchanged and does not create a user namespace. `sudo unroot unpack --native` creates this mode.
* *Single-ID ownership* maps only the invoking UID and GID to namespace ID 0. Request it explicitly for an unmanaged rootfs with `unroot enter --single ROOT`.

`unroot enter ROOT` reads the stored mode before namespace creation. A rich root must still belong to the same host UID and GID, and its exact subordinate ranges must remain assigned. A native root requires host root privileges. Unroot never silently chooses a replacement map, rewrites ownership, or changes modes.

An existing rootfs with no metadata is not guessed. Use `unroot enter --single ROOT` for a single-owner tree, or `sudo unroot enter --native ROOT` to state that its host-visible ownership is intentional. Neither unmanaged form creates `.unroot` metadata. Use `unroot unpack` when a portable managed rootfs is desired.

Rich ownership requires suitable subordinate-ID allocations and the `unroot-util`, `newuidmap`, and `newgidmap` helpers. `unroot-util` must be installed beside `unroot`. When built with libsubid, it uses the host's configured subordinate-ID provider; otherwise it reads `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid` directly. Each rich root requires one contiguous subordinate UID range and one contiguous subordinate GID range at least as large as its selected ID count.

topic:filesystem-setup.name: filesystem-setup
topic:filesystem-setup.title: Filesystem setup
topic:filesystem-setup.description:
Rooted entry prepares a private mount tree, enters *ROOT* with `chroot(2)`, mounts a private `/proc`, and performs the enabled minimal filesystem setup described under `FILESYSTEM SETUP`. Both rich and native entry retain private mount and PID namespaces. *ROOT* must be a distinct root filesystem; `enter` rejects any path that resolves to the host `/`.

`--map` bind-mounts an absolute host path at the same absolute path inside the root filesystem. `--map-ro` accepts either *SOURCE* for the same-path shorthand or *SOURCE:DESTINATION* for an explicit destination, and requires the resulting bind mount to be read-only. Directory mappings also protect nested mounts recursively. Both options may be repeated and apply only to `enter`.

topic:foreign-execution.name: foreign-execution
topic:foreign-execution.title: Foreign-architecture execution
topic:foreign-execution.description:
`unroot` compares the requested executable's ELF architecture with the host and selects the conventional static QEMU user-mode emulator when they differ. The executable or resolved shebang interpreter is authoritative; Unroot does not maintain distro subarchitecture profiles, choose compiler flags, or select rootfs variants.

Rich roots use a private `binfmt_misc` instance. Unroot stages the static emulator and its own wrapper beneath `.unroot/bin`, registers the target architecture only inside the new namespace, and removes the entire registration naturally when the namespace exits. `--qemu-cpu` is available here for an explicit QEMU CPU and feature specification.

Native roots use host `binfmt_misc`, because there is no user namespace in which to create a private instance. On foreign entry, Unroot first reuses any enabled fixed-interpreter handler with the exact target ELF magic and mask. If none exists, it registers a handler named `unroot-ARCH` using a trusted, root-owned, non-writable static QEMU from standard system directories. The registration uses the kernel's fix-binary behavior so the interpreter remains available after `chroot`, and remains active for the current boot. Unroot refuses to replace a conflicting handler.

An explicit `--qemu` used with native mode must resolve to a trusted absolute path whose file and parent hierarchy are root-owned and not group- or other-writable. Native mode does not accept `--qemu-cpu`, because a host-global registration cannot safely carry per-rootfs CPU policy. Rootfs metadata never supplies a host emulator path or raw registration string.

Use `--emulation never` when foreign execution must fail rather than start QEMU. QEMU overrides apply only when the target architecture differs from the host. Unroot includes ELF class and byte order in target identity and rejects recognized but unsupported combinations rather than choosing an approximate emulator.

During a foreign-architecture build, Portage's `pid-sandbox` may create another PID namespace and trigger a QEMU linux-user failure: `qemu: qemu_thread_create: Invalid argument`. Foreign Gentoo and Funtoo builds should disable only this Portage feature with `FEATURES="-pid-sandbox"` in `/etc/portage/make.conf`. Native-architecture builds do not need this workaround. This is an upstream QEMU limitation tracked at https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/issues/172 and https://github.com/danielrobbins/unroot/issues/13; Unroot does not silently rewrite distribution build policy.

Private `binfmt_misc` instances require Linux 6.7 or newer and permission from the surrounding runtime. Native foreign execution works on older kernels that support ordinary host `binfmt_misc`, but requires host root privileges to mount or register it when no compatible handler already exists.

topic:security-model.name: security-model
topic:security-model.title: SECURITY MODEL
topic:security-model.description:
`unroot` is intended for root filesystems and commands that you trust. It is not a sandbox for hostile code.

Rich roots and rooted `--single` use a user namespace, so namespace root capabilities do not become host root privileges. Native mode deliberately uses host root and must be requested explicitly for an unmanaged rootfs or recorded in managed metadata. Native foreign execution may add a host-global QEMU registration for the current boot; it uses only an enabled compatible handler or a trusted static system executable and will not overwrite a conflict.

Every mode creates private mount and PID namespaces. Mount changes remain private to the process tree. Unroot deliberately shares the host network, IPC namespace, hostname, cgroup hierarchy, kernel, and available hardware interfaces. It does not install a syscall filter, impose resource limits, or create an AppArmor or SELinux policy.

Explicit bind mappings and device resources remain backed by host resources. Managed resolver and hosts injections are copied from trusted host files and remain ordinary writable rootfs files while active; the managed `mtab` injection is a rootfs-local compatibility symlink. `UNROOT_FEATURES=+devbind` exposes the complete host `/dev` tree and should be enabled only when that access is intended.

option:enter.single.name: enter.single
option:enter.single.title: --single
option:enter.single.description: Enter an unmanaged rootfs with a single UID and GID mapping. The invoking host user and group become namespace ID 0; no subordinate IDs are required. This mode conflicts with `--native` and with any ownership metadata already recorded for *ROOT*.

option:enter.native.name: enter.native
option:enter.native.title: --native
option:enter.native.description: Enter an unmanaged host-owned rootfs, or create a native rootfs with `unpack`. Requires host root privileges. It conflicts with a managed rich ownership record.

option:archive.force.name: archive.force
option:archive.force.title: --force
option:archive.force.description: Allow `pack` or `unpack` to continue after a recoverable libarchive metadata warning or a reported destination metadata limitation. The warning is still displayed. This option does not override unsafe archive structure, ownership-map violations, corrupt data, or archive-engine failures.

option:unpack.id-count.name: unpack.id-count
option:unpack.id-count.title: --id-count COUNT
option:unpack.id-count.description: Set the number of subordinate UIDs and GIDs represented by a new rich root. The default is 65535. *COUNT* excludes rootfs ID 0, so a count of 100000 represents rootfs IDs 0 through 100000. The invoking account must have contiguous subordinate UID and GID allocations of at least this size. This option cannot be combined with `--native`.

option:process.cwd.name: process.cwd
option:process.cwd.title: --cwd DIRECTORY
option:process.cwd.description: Set the command's working directory inside *ROOT*.

option:process.env.name: process.env
option:process.env.title: --env KEY=VALUE
option:process.env.description: Set an environment variable for the target command. May be repeated.

option:process.persist-env.name: process.persist-env
option:process.persist-env.title: --persist-env NAMES
option:process.persist-env.description: Copy a comma-separated list of variables from the host environment.

option:process.no-default-env.name: process.no-default-env
option:process.no-default-env.title: --no-default-env
option:process.no-default-env.description: Do not supply Unroot's deterministic target `PATH`. Explicit `--env` and `--persist-env` selections are unaffected.

option:enter.map.name: enter.map
option:enter.map.title: --map PATH
option:enter.map.description: Bind an absolute host path at the same path inside *ROOT*. May be repeated.

option:enter.map-ro.name: enter.map-ro
option:enter.map-ro.title: --map-ro SOURCE
option:enter.map-ro.description: Bind an absolute host path inside *ROOT*, then make that mount and any nested mounts read-only. With no destination, the source is mounted at the same absolute path. May be repeated.

option:unpack.inject.name: unpack.inject
option:unpack.inject.title: --inject EXCLUSIONS
option:unpack.inject.description: Disable one or more default injections during `unpack`. Accepts `-hosts`, `-resolv.conf`, `-mtab`, a comma-separated combination, or `-*` for all defaults. Use the equals form, such as `--inject=-hosts` or `--inject=-hosts,-mtab`, so a negative value is not mistaken for an option. May be repeated. Positive and custom injection specifications belong to `unroot inject add`.

option:enter.emulation.name: enter.emulation
option:enter.emulation.title: --emulation MODE
option:enter.emulation.description: Set the foreign-execution policy. `auto`, the default, uses a static QEMU user-mode emulator when the target ELF architecture differs from the host. `never` rejects a foreign target instead.

option:enter.qemu.name: enter.qemu
option:enter.qemu.title: --qemu PATH
option:enter.qemu.description: Use the specified static QEMU user-mode emulator for foreign execution. Rich mode may use an executable path or a name on the host `PATH`. Native mode requires a trusted root-owned system path. The emulator itself must be executable by the host architecture.

option:enter.qemu-cpu.name: enter.qemu-cpu
option:enter.qemu-cpu.title: --qemu-cpu SPEC
option:enter.qemu-cpu.description: Pass `-cpu` *SPEC* to QEMU for private rich-mode foreign execution. The specification may be a model alone or a model followed by QEMU feature properties, such as `max,sve=on,sve256=on`. Native mode rejects this option because its QEMU handler is host-global.

option:global.help.name: global.help
option:global.help.title: --help, -h
option:global.help.description: Show help for the selected action.

option:global.debug.name: global.debug
option:global.debug.title: --debug
option:global.debug.description:
The global `--debug` option must precede the action and enables structured diagnostic logging:

```console
$ unroot --debug enter ~/rootfs -- /bin/true
```

topic:mount-features-overview.name: mount-features-overview
topic:mount-features-overview.title: Feature selection
topic:mount-features-overview.description:
`UNROOT_FEATURES` adjusts filesystem setup with a comma-separated list of feature names. Prefix a name with `-` to disable it or `+` to enable it. `-*` disables all optional features before later tokens are applied.

Rooted mode enables `sys`, `devpts`, `shm`, and `run` by default. `/sys` is a recursive read-only bind of the host sysfs so topology and hardware-discovery tools can inspect the running machine without gaining a writable control surface. `/proc` is always mounted privately and cannot be disabled. `devbind` is disabled by default.

Bind mounts retain the host source's inode ownership and permissions. In rootless modes, host IDs outside the namespace map appear as the overflow `nobody` identity, and namespace root does not gain host-root access. The `/proc` mount point itself may similarly display overflow ownership because of its kernel-provided root inode; namespaced process entries such as `/proc/self/status` still report the mapped process identity.

For example, this disables the private shared-memory mount and enables the full device bind:

```console
$ UNROOT_FEATURES=-shm,+devbind unroot enter ~/rootfs
```

feature:devpts.name: devpts
feature:devpts.title: devpts
feature:devpts.description: Mount a private `/dev/pts` for pseudo-terminal support.

feature:sys.name: sys
feature:sys.title: sys
feature:sys.description: Bind the host `/sys` into *ROOT* as a recursive read-only mount.

feature:devbind.name: devbind
feature:devbind.title: devbind
feature:devbind.description: Bind the complete host `/dev` tree into the root filesystem.

topic:diagnostics.name: diagnostics
topic:diagnostics.title: DIAGNOSTICS
topic:diagnostics.description:
When namespace creation or setup is denied, `unroot` reports the failed operation, system error, and observable policy context. This includes disabled user-namespace sysctls, AppArmor's unprivileged-user-namespace restriction, an enforcing SELinux context, seccomp state, and an outer-container policy hint when available.

Rich preflight errors identify missing subordinate allocations, `unroot-util`, `newuidmap`, or `newgidmap` before the destination rootfs is created. Native-mode errors distinguish missing host root privileges, conflicting metadata, unavailable trusted QEMU, and conflicting `binfmt_misc` handlers.

Use the global `--debug` option for detailed structured setup events.

topic:exit-status.name: exit-status
topic:exit-status.title: EXIT STATUS
topic:exit-status.description: After successful setup, `unroot` returns the target command's exit status. Commands terminated by a signal use the conventional `128 + signal` result. `pack` and `unpack` return the archive helper's result after namespace setup. Argument, namespace, ownership, mount, archive, emulation, and execution setup failures return a nonzero status with a diagnostic on standard error.

topic:requirements.name: requirements
topic:requirements.title: REQUIREMENTS
topic:requirements.description:
Rooted `--single` and rich rootfs entry require Linux with unprivileged user namespaces enabled by the kernel and permitted by the active AppArmor, SELinux, seccomp, and outer-container policy.

Rich ownership additionally requires `unroot-util` installed beside `unroot`, `/usr/bin/newuidmap`, `/usr/bin/newgidmap`, and a subordinate UID and GID allocation from the host's configured provider. Builds without libsubid support use `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid` directly.

Native ownership requires host root privileges and Linux mount and PID namespace support. `--map-ro` additionally requires `mount_setattr(2)`, available in Linux 5.12 or newer.

Private foreign execution additionally requires Linux 6.7 or newer and a compatible static `qemu-*-static` user emulator. Native foreign execution requires host `binfmt_misc` and a trusted static QEMU when no compatible handler is already registered.

Archive inspection, `pack`, and `unpack` require `unroot-util` installed beside `unroot`. Libarchive is a mandatory build and runtime dependency of the helper, and every build verifies that the linked library can read and write POSIX ACLs and extended attributes. The build fails if libarchive is unavailable or if the linked library or build probe filesystem cannot preserve either metadata type. Set `UNROOT_LIBARCHIVE_PROBE_DIR` when `/tmp` is not a suitable probe filesystem.

Adding, removing, or clearing injections also requires the sibling `unroot-util`; it performs mapped file installation and restoration under the ownership policy selected by the static engine. Listing the registry does not modify the rootfs.

file:root-meta.name: root-meta
file:root-meta.title: ROOT/.unroot/meta.json
file:root-meta.description: Authoritative per-rootfs ownership and execution metadata maintained by `unroot`. Unmanaged `enter --single` and `enter --native` do not create it.

file:root-lock.name: root-lock
file:root-lock.title: ROOT/.unroot/meta.lock
file:root-lock.description: Coordination lock used while a managed root filesystem is initialized.

file:injection-registry.name: injection-registry
file:injection-registry.title: ROOT/.unroot/injections/
file:injection-registry.description: Private registry and preserved originals for durable rootfs injections. This tree is never included directly in a packed rootfs; `pack` substitutes each preserved original at its portable path.

file:root-bin.name: root-bin
file:root-bin.title: ROOT/.unroot/bin/
file:root-bin.description: Versioned wrapper and emulator staging paths used by private rich-mode foreign execution.

file:subordinate-ids.name: subordinate-ids
file:subordinate-ids.title: /etc/subuid, /etc/subgid
file:subordinate-ids.description: Host allocations used for rich ownership when `unroot-util` is built without libsubid support.

file:unroot-util.name: unroot-util
file:unroot-util.title: .../unroot-util
file:unroot-util.description: Dynamically linked host-integration helper used for rich subordinate-ID discovery. It must be installed in the same directory as `unroot`.
